The Larkspur Archive is a digitized-collection platform for Bellweather
Books: scanning, OCR, searchable metadata, and an online viewer. The OCR
pipeline uses a remote OCR API over local OCR (decision d-004, informed by
the ocr-comparison notes); a later latency benchmark (s-006) showed archival
page scans running far below the assumed throughput, which sent Dev and
Silas back to preprocessing. The viewer is IIIF-based (decision d-011),
prototyped in s-010.

Team: Silas Brandt (data), June Park (interface), Dev Okonkwo (OCR pipeline),
Odessa Klein (user research). Rowan Ellery is the client sponsor; Quill &
Marrow advised the metadata descriptions. Mid-project review with Bellweather
is m-007.

As of mid-June the project is active: OCR continues at the corrected rate and
the IIIF viewer is in integration.

id: d-004
genre: decisions
title: "Larkspur Archive routes OCR through a remote API"
created: 2026-03-12
provenance: hand-authored
tags: [larkspur, ocr]
status: accepted
related:
  - type: influenced_by
    to: references/ocr-comparison.md
  - type: mentions

---

Context: Bellweather's archive scans number in the tens of thousands of
pages; OCR throughput sets the digitization schedule.

Options considered: local OCR on the studio's machines; a remote OCR API.

Decision: route Larkspur OCR through a remote API — roughly four times local
throughput at an absorbable per-page cost, informed by the ocr-comparison
benchmark notes.

Consequences: the digitization schedule holds; throughput is assumed to scale
linearly with scan volume. Later contradicted by the latency benchmark in
s-006, which found archival page scans far below the assumed rate.

Silas benchmarked the OCR pipeline against the ocr-comparison assumption: on
real archival page scans — foxed paper, old typefaces — throughput ran at
roughly forty percent of the assumed rate once image preprocessing landed.
The linearity assumption behind d-004 does not hold for archival material;
batching and preprocessing now set the schedule, not API capacity.

id: ocr-comparison
genre: references
title: "Local OCR vs remote OCR API — benchmark notes"
created: 2026-03-10
provenance: hand-authored
tags: [ocr, benchmark]
source: "internal benchmark notes, Q1 tooling review"
---

Comparing local OCR against a remote OCR API on sample scans: the remote API
sustained roughly four times the local throughput at a per-page cost the
studio could absorb, with better layout detection on old typefaces.
Assumption on record: throughput scales linearly with scan volume.

Informed d-004. The linearity assumption is what s-006 later challenged.

final_answer:
**Larkspur OCR Story Synthesis**

**Original Assumption** (from `decisions/d-004.md` and `references/ocr-comparison.md`):
- The team assumed OCR throughput would scale *linearly* with scan volume when using a remote OCR API
- Benchmark notes showed the remote API sustained "roughly four times the local throughput at a per-page cost the studio could absorb" — this linear-scaling assumption was explicitly recorded and informed decision d-004 to route Larkspur OCR through a remote API

**Benchmark Finding** (from `sessions/s-006.md`):
- Silas benchmarked the pipeline on *real archival page scans* (foxed paper, old typefaces)
- Throughput ran at **"roughly forty percent of the assumed rate"** once image preprocessing landed
- "The linearity assumption behind d-004 does not hold for archival material; batching and preprocessing now set the schedule, not API capacity"

**Schedule Consequence** (from `meetings/m-007.md`):
- At the mid-project review with Bellweather (m-007), the OCR latency findings were walked through
- "Archival scans run at roughly forty percent of the assumed rate, **so the digitization schedule stretches**"
- The project remained active as of mid-June with "OCR continuing at the corrected rate" (`projects/larkspur-archive.md`)
